prompt.context: Penguins have evolved. Now they can talk and they are organized as an advanced society. The ambassador of Penguinland (former Antarctica) has reached out to Bain & Company because he is worried about the growing population growth of penguins. Currently, there are about 23 million penguins and the population is growing 32% per year.
prompt.question: How many penguins can live at Penguinland and what is the best way to accommodate everyone?

clarifying_info.q: Are there predators that threaten the penguins?
clarifying_info.a: The penguins negotiated with all predators. The polar bears now live in a Zoo in San Diego and the whales live at Sea World.

clarifying_info.q: Is there enough food for all penguins?
clarifying_info.a: There is plenty of food all over the ocean — more than enough to feed every penguin.

clarifying_info.q: What are the penguins' living habits and space requirements?
clarifying_info.a: They are all married and have a baby penguin. They need space for both penguins to live and a nest for the baby. Penguins do not need space for leisure — only space to sleep. Penguins must eat every day.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of Penguinland (Antarctica)?
clarifying_info.a: See Exhibit 1 — you may approximate the map to a square.

clarifying_info.q: How fast can penguins walk and for how long each day?
clarifying_info.a: Penguins only walk and eat during the day; they must sleep the whole night. The longest day of the year has 22 hours of sunlight (shortest day has only 2 hours). The average penguin leg is 20 cm; the average human leg is 1 m. Humans walk at an average of 5 km/h.

clarifying_info.q: How long does it take a penguin to eat?
clarifying_info.a: Even if a penguin stays in the ocean for only 1 second, it is enough to eat one fish.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of a penguin and a nest?
clarifying_info.a: Penguin size = 1 m²; Nest size = 1 m².

exhibits.title: Penguinland Map
exhibits.shows: A map of Penguinland (Antarctica) with a scale bar indicating 4,000 km across the continent.

framework: Determine the total area of Penguinland (Antarctica)
Identify key constraints on where penguins can actually live (food access, predators, habits)
Calculate how far from the ocean a penguin can survive given walking speed and daily time budget
Derive the total habitable coastal band area
Estimate how many penguin families fit in the habitable area given space requirements and road needs
Compare to current and projected population

questions.prompt: Calculate the total area of Penguinland.
questions.guidance: Candidate should approximate the map (Exhibit 1) as a square with 4,000 km sides.

math.setup: Area of Antarctica ≈ square with side 4,000 km

questions.prompt: How far from the ocean can a penguin live?
questions.guidance: Candidate must derive penguin walking speed from leg length ratio, then apply the shortest-day constraint: penguins must walk to the ocean and back in one day. Using the shortest day (2 hours of sunlight) is the binding constraint.

math.setup: Penguin speed as fraction of human speed based on leg length; round-trip to ocean must fit within shortest day
steps: Penguin leg = 20 cm = 0.2 m; Human leg = 1 m → ratio = 1/5
Penguins must walk to ocean AND back → 1 hour each way
math.answer: Penguins can live at most 1 km from the ocean

questions.prompt: Calculate the total habitable coastal band area.
questions.guidance: The habitable strip is a 1 km band around the 4,000 km × 4,000 km square continent. Approximate as 4 rectangles (one per side), each 4,000 km long and 1 km wide.

math.setup: 4 coastal strips, each 4,000 km × 1 km (corner overlaps negligible)
steps: (Precise: two sides = 4,000 × 1 and two sides = 3,998 × 1 → 15,996 km² ≈ 16,000 km²)

questions.prompt: How many penguins can be accommodated in the habitable area?
questions.guidance: Each family unit is 1 male + 1 female + 1 baby = 3 penguins. The layout requires 2 roads (1 m each) plus 3 penguin/nest spaces (1 m² each), totalling 5 m² per family. Candidate should propose the road-sharing layout: two parallel 1 m roads flanking penguin pairs with nests.

math.setup: Optimal layout: 2 roads (1 m wide each) + 1 male space (1 m²) + 1 female space (1 m²) + 1 nest (1 m²) = 5 m² per family of 3

recommendation: Penguinland can sustainably accommodate approximately 9.6 billion penguins — far above the current 23 million population
The key constraint is the 1 km habitable coastal band (determined by walking speed and shortest day)
The optimal settlement layout uses a 5 m² per family unit (male + female + nest/baby + 2 roads), yielding 3 penguins per 5 m²
risks: Shortest-day constraint is binding — population in interior regions is zero
Road infrastructure must be planned from the outset; ad hoc settlement will reduce capacity
Seasonal variation in daylight could affect food access at higher latitudes
Long-run population growth at 32%/yr would reach 9.6B in roughly 17 years
next_steps: Map actual Antarctic coastline to refine the 16,000 km² coastal band estimate
Design urban planning rules enforcing the 2-road layout
Monitor annual population growth to project when capacity becomes a real constraint
